title: Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer

toc.title: 8.1 Thermal energy, heat and temperature; thermal equilibrium and the zeroth law
8.3 Conduction, convection and radiation; black-body radiation and the Stefan–Boltzmann law

html:
Heat is the first idea in physics that everyone thinks they understand and almost everyone gets slightly wrong. Heat is not temperature, temperature is not "how hot something feels", and a bathtub of warm water contains far more thermal energy than a cup of boiling tea. Of the 7 Heat and Thermodynamics questions in the paper (official weightage), we estimate about 2 come from this chapter. They are usually one definition (the zeroth law, a thermometric property), one comparison (which thermometer for which job), and one calculation — a Stefan-law ratio, a composite slab, or a cooling curve.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference (J); temperature measures the average molecular kinetic energy; thermal energy is the total internal energy.
  • Zeroth law: if A is in equilibrium with B and B with C, then A is in equilibrium with C — the basis of thermometry.
  • T(\text{K}) = \theta(^\circ\text{C}) + 273, \theta_F = \frac{9}{5}\theta_C + 32; -40^\circ is the same on both scales.
  • Thermometers: liquid-in-glass (apparent expansion), resistance (R=R_0(1+\alpha\theta)), thermocouple (Seebeck emf), radiation (Stefan–Boltzmann). Know one advantage and one limitation of each.
  • Conduction: H=\frac{Q}{t}=\frac{kA(\theta_1-\theta_2)}{L}; thermal resistance L/kA adds in series.
  • Stefan–Boltzmann: P=\varepsilon\sigma AT^4, \sigma=5.67\times10^{-8} W m⁻² K⁻⁴; net loss \varepsilon\sigma A(T^4-T_s^4).
  • Wien's law: \lambda_{max}T=2.9\times10^{-3} m K.
  • Newton's law of cooling: rate of loss \propto (body temperature − surroundings), giving an exponential fall.

8.1 Thermal energy, heat and temperature; thermal equilibrium and the zeroth law

Three words that are not the same

Quantity What it is Unit Depends on
Temperature a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules of a body K (or °C) how fast the molecules move
Thermal energy the total internal energy of the body — the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of all its molecules J temperature, mass, state
Heat energy in transit from one body to another because of a temperature difference J the process, not the body

Temperature is a state variable: a body "has" a temperature. Heat is not something a body contains — it is energy crossing a boundary, so a body "gains" or "loses" heat, it does not "have" heat. What a body contains is internal (thermal) energy.

This is why a bathtub of water at 40 °C has far more thermal energy than a cup of tea at 90 °C: it has many more molecules, even though each molecule moves more slowly.

For a gas, temperature is directly tied to molecular motion:

\frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2} = \frac{3}{2}kT

so the root-mean-square speed grows as \sqrt{T}. Doubling the absolute temperature multiplies the average kinetic energy per molecule by 2, and the rms speed by \sqrt{2}.

Heat is not "hotness"

Two statements that are wrong and appear as options every year: - "A body contains heat." No — it contains internal energy; heat is energy being transferred. - "Temperature is the total kinetic energy." No — it is the average kinetic energy per molecule.

Thermal contact and thermal equilibrium

When two bodies at different temperatures are placed in thermal contact (so energy can pass between them), energy flows from the hotter to the colder one until both reach the same temperature. At that point there is no net transfer of energy and the bodies are in thermal equilibrium. The molecules are still moving and energy is still exchanged at the microscopic level — the exchange rates are simply equal in both directions.

Zeroth law of thermodynamics

If body A is in thermal equilibrium with body B, and body B is in thermal equilibrium with body C, then A is in thermal equilibrium with C.

The law looks obvious, but it is what makes temperature a meaningful quantity: it says that "being at the same temperature" is transitive. Its practical use is thermometry — a thermometer (B) placed in contact with a patient (A) reaches equilibrium with the patient; the thermometer's reading then tells us the patient's temperature, and two patients that both match the same thermometer match each other.

Temperature scales

Scale Ice point Steam point Absolute zero Size of one degree
Celsius 0 °C 100 °C −273.15 °C 1 °C
Fahrenheit 32 °F 212 °F −459.67 °F 1 °F = 5/9 °C
Kelvin 273.15 K 373.15 K 0 K 1 K = 1 °C

\theta_F = \frac{9}{5}\theta_C + 32, \qquad T = \theta_C + 273.15

The two fixed points give the conversion by proportion:

\frac{\theta_C}{100} = \frac{\theta_F - 32}{180} = \frac{T - 273.15}{100}

Only one temperature is numerically the same on the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales: put \theta_C = \theta_F = x in the conversion:

x = \frac{9}{5}x + 32 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\frac{4}{5}x = 32 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = -40

so −40 °C = −40 °F.

Absolute zero and the Kelvin scale

Cooling a gas at constant volume lowers its pressure in proportion to the temperature on the Celsius scale. Extrapolating to zero pressure gives −273.15 °C, the lowest temperature possible — absolute zero. On the Kelvin scale this is 0 K, and no temperature can be lower because a negative absolute temperature would mean negative molecular kinetic energy.

The Kelvin scale is the SI scale because its zero is a true zero: ratios of temperatures are meaningful, which is exactly what the Stefan and Wien laws need. "The temperature doubled" only has a meaning in kelvin.

The triple point of water — the temperature and pressure at which ice, water and vapour coexist — is 273.16 K, and it is the modern fixed point that defines the kelvin.

Worked example 8.1 — converting a temperature

Problem. Normal body temperature is 37 °C. Express it in °F and in K. At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit readings agree?

Solution. \theta_F = \frac{9}{5}(37) + 32 = 66.6 + 32 = 98.6 °F. T = 37 + 273 = 310 K.

For equal readings, \theta_F = \theta_C: \theta = \frac{9}{5}\theta + 32, so \theta = -40. The two scales agree at −40 degrees.

8.2 Thermometers

What a thermometer must do

A thermometer works through a thermometric property — a physical property that changes steadily and reproducibly with temperature. The common ones are the length of a liquid column, the electrical resistance of a metal, the emf of a thermocouple, the pressure of a gas at constant volume, and the radiation emitted by a surface.

A good thermometer should be:

  1. sensitive — a large change in the property for a small change in temperature;
  2. accurate and reproducible — the same temperature gives the same reading every time;
  3. linear — equal temperature steps give equal scale steps, or the non-linearity must be calibrated out;
  4. quick — a small heat capacity and good thermal contact, so it does not disturb what it measures;
  5. wide in range, robust, and safe.

No single instrument has all of these, which is why the paper asks "which thermometer would you use for …".

Liquid-in-glass thermometer

Principle. A liquid expands more than the glass that contains it. What we read is the apparent expansion of the liquid, which is its real expansion minus the expansion of the glass bulb and tube. Because the glass also expands, two thermometers made of different glasses can read slightly differently at the same temperature — a real limitation.

Liquid Range Advantages Limitations
Mercury −39 °C to 357 °C opaque, does not wet glass, good conductor, wide range toxic, expensive, freezes at −39 °C, cannot read low temperatures
Alcohol −115 °C to 78 °C cheap, very low freezing point, large expansion coloured (needs dye), wets the glass, evaporates, cannot read high temperatures

Other limitations of any liquid-in-glass thermometer: fragile; slow to respond; must be read where it is (no remote reading); parallax error; the stem must be immersed to the correct depth; a large bulb takes heat from a small sample.

The clinical thermometer is a special mercury thermometer with a range of only 35–42 °C, a constriction just above the bulb so that the mercury does not run back when it is removed from the patient, and a least count of 0.1 °C. It must be shaken down before use.

Resistance thermometer

Principle. The electrical resistance of a metal rises with temperature:

R = R_0(1 + \alpha\theta)

where R_0 is the resistance at 0 °C and \alpha the temperature coefficient of resistance. Platinum is used because it is chemically stable and its resistance changes very reproducibly over a wide range.

  • Range: about −200 °C to 850 °C.
  • Advantages: very accurate and reproducible; wide range; the reading can be sent down a cable and recorded automatically; no parallax; can be made very stable over years.
  • Limitations: needs a power supply and a bridge circuit; the current heats the element slightly (self-heating); slower than a thermocouple; more expensive; \alpha is not perfectly constant over the whole range.

Thermocouple thermometer

Principle. Join two different metals at both ends. If the two junctions are at different temperatures, a small emf appears in the circuit — the Seebeck effect. The emf is roughly proportional to the temperature difference between the junctions:

\varepsilon \approx \alpha(T_{hot} - T_{cold})

  • Range: about −200 °C to 1600 °C, depending on the metal pair.
  • Advantages: the junction can be tiny, so it responds quickly, has a very small heat capacity and can measure the temperature of a single point; it is rugged, cheap, and can be read remotely.
  • Limitations: the emf is only a few tens of microvolts per degree, so amplification is needed; the cold junction must be kept at a known temperature (or electronically compensated); the relation is non-linear; the calibration drifts as the metals age.

Radiation thermometer (pyrometer)

Principle. Every hot body radiates energy at a rate that grows very rapidly with temperature. A pyrometer measures the radiation received and converts it to a temperature using the Stefan–Boltzmann law (total radiation pyrometer) or by comparing the intensities at two wavelengths (ratio pyrometer).

  • Range: about 800 °C to 3000 °C and beyond.
  • Advantages: no contact, so it can measure a moving furnace belt, molten metal, a rotating shaft or a distant star; it does not disturb the object; it can be very fast.
  • Limitations: it needs the emissivity of the surface to be known (a shiny surface reads too low); it needs a clear line of sight (smoke, dust and steam interfere); it is not usable at low temperatures where the radiated power is small; it is expensive.

Comparison

Thermometer Principle Typical range Main advantage Main limitation
Mercury in glass apparent expansion −39 to 357 °C simple, cheap, direct reading fragile, limited range, not remote
Alcohol in glass apparent expansion −115 to 78 °C works at very low temperatures wets glass, cannot go high
Platinum resistance R=R_0(1+\alpha\theta) −200 to 850 °C very accurate and reproducible needs power, slow, self-heating
Thermocouple Seebeck emf −200 to 1600 °C tiny junction, fast, wide range needs cold-junction compensation, small emf
Radiation pyrometer Stefan–Boltzmann 800 to 3000 °C no contact, very high temperatures depends on emissivity, line of sight
Choosing a thermometer in an MCQ

Ask three questions in order: How hot? (range), Can I touch it? (contact or not), How fast and how small? (response). A furnace wall that is moving → pyrometer. The temperature inside a grain store, logged for a month → resistance. The temperature at one point inside a running engine → thermocouple. A patient → clinical mercury thermometer.

8.3 Conduction, convection and radiation; black-body radiation and the Stefan–Boltzmann law

Heat always moves from a hotter region to a colder one, and it does so by three mechanisms that can act together.

Mode What moves Needs a medium? Example
Conduction energy passed from molecule to molecule (and by free electrons in metals) yes a metal spoon in hot tea
Convection the hot fluid itself moves yes, a fluid sea breeze, boiling water
Radiation electromagnetic waves no heat from the Sun reaching the Earth

Conduction and the temperature gradient

In steady state, the temperature at each point of a rod no longer changes with time, and the rate of heat flow is

H = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{kA(\theta_1-\theta_2)}{L}

where k is the thermal conductivity of the material (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹), A the cross-section, L the length and \theta_1-\theta_2 the temperature difference between the ends.

The quantity (\theta_1-\theta_2)/L is the temperature gradient; in the limit of a thin slice,

H = -kA\frac{d\theta}{dx}

The minus sign says heat flows down the temperature gradient, from hot to cold.

Material k (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Silver 406
Copper 385
Aluminium 205
Steel 50
Glass 0.8
Water 0.6
Wood 0.15
Air 0.024

Metals conduct well because their free electrons carry energy quickly through the lattice as well as the vibrating ions. Air conducts very poorly, which is why wool, feathers, thermocol and double glazing — all of which trap air — are good insulators.

Composite slabs and thermal resistance

A slab of thickness L and conductivity k has a thermal resistance

R_{th} = \frac{L}{kA}

and the conduction equation becomes H = \Delta\theta/R_{th} — exactly the form of Ohm's law, with H playing the part of current and \Delta\theta of voltage. For slabs in series (heat crosses them one after another) the resistances add:

H = \frac{A(\theta_1-\theta_n)}{\frac{L_1}{k_1}+\frac{L_2}{k_2}+\cdots+\frac{L_n}{k_n}}

For rods in parallel, the conductances kA/L add.

Worked example 8.2 — a composite wall

Problem. A wall consists of a 2.0 cm copper layer (k=400 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) and a 2.0 cm insulating layer (k=0.40 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹), each of area 1.0 m². The outside faces are at 100 °C and 0 °C. Find the heat current and the temperature at the interface.

Solution. In series,

H = \frac{A\,\Delta\theta}{\frac{L_1}{k_1}+\frac{L_2}{k_2}} = \frac{(1.0)(100)}{0.020/400 + 0.020/0.40} = \frac{100}{5.0\times10^{-5}+0.050} \approx 2.0\times10^3\ \text{W}

Across the copper the drop is H L_1/(k_1A) = 2000\times5.0\times10^{-5} = 0.10 °C, so the interface is at 99.9 °C. Almost the whole 100 °C falls across the insulator: the temperature profile is steepest in the poorer conductor.

Convection

In convection the fluid itself moves and carries its thermal energy with it.

  • Natural convection occurs because a warmed fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises, while cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place. It needs gravity (or an equivalent acceleration); in a freely falling lift or an orbiting spacecraft there is no natural convection.
  • Forced convection uses a pump or a fan: central heating, a car radiator, blood circulation.
Example What happens
Sea breeze (day) land heats faster than the sea; air over the land rises; cooler air flows in from the sea
Land breeze (night) the sea stays warmer; air over the sea rises; air flows out from the land
Room heater placed low, so warm air rises and circulates through the room
Air conditioner placed high, so cool dense air sinks through the room
Chimney hot smoke rises, drawing fresh air in at the bottom
Monsoon summer heating of the land draws moist air in from the Indian Ocean

Newton's law of cooling

For a body cooling in air, when the excess temperature over the surroundings is small, the rate of loss of heat is proportional to that excess:

\frac{dQ}{dt} = -k(\theta - \theta_s)

Since dQ = mc\,d\theta for the body,

mc\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -k(\theta-\theta_s) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta = \theta_s + (\theta_0-\theta_s)e^{-kt/mc}

The temperature falls exponentially towards the surroundings' temperature, never quite reaching it. Equal time intervals remove equal fractions of the remaining excess, not equal numbers of degrees.

Newton's law is only for small excess temperatures

The law assumes the heat is carried away by natural convection and radiation together in a way that is roughly linear in the excess temperature. At large excess temperatures radiation dominates (and goes as T^4), so the simple exponential fails. It also assumes the surroundings do not warm up, and no evaporation.

Radiation

Thermal radiation is electromagnetic radiation emitted by every body because of its temperature. Its properties:

  • it needs no medium — it crosses a vacuum, which is how the Sun's energy reaches us;
  • it travels at the speed of light and obeys the same laws as light (reflection, refraction, polarisation);
  • at everyday temperatures it is mostly infrared; above about 500 °C a body glows dull red, and at about 1500 °C it is white-hot.

Prevost's theory: every body emits radiation at all times, whatever its temperature, and also absorbs radiation from its surroundings. If it emits faster than it absorbs, it cools; if it absorbs faster, it warms; at equal temperatures the two rates are equal.

Black body and emissivity

Black body

A black body is an ideal body that absorbs all radiation of every wavelength falling on it — its absorptivity is 1 — and, at a given temperature, emits more energy than any other body.

A small hole in a hollow cavity is the closest practical black body: radiation that enters the hole is reflected many times inside and is almost completely absorbed. Soot and lampblack come close (\varepsilon\approx0.95).

The emissivity \varepsilon of a real surface is the ratio of the energy it emits to the energy a black body of the same area and temperature would emit:

\varepsilon = \frac{P_{real}}{P_{black}} \qquad (0 \le \varepsilon \le 1)

Emissivity and absorptivity

Kirchhoff's law: at a given temperature and wavelength, a good absorber is also a good emitter, so \varepsilon=\alpha. A blackened surface (high \varepsilon, high \alpha) heats quickly in sunshine and cools quickly at night. A shiny white surface (low \varepsilon, low \alpha) stays cooler in the sun and cools slowly after sunset. Do not mix the two: absorptivity is about radiation arriving, emissivity about radiation leaving.

Stefan–Boltzmann law

The total energy radiated per second by a black body of area A at absolute temperature T is

P = \sigma A T^4

and for a real surface

P = \varepsilon\sigma A T^4

with the Stefan constant

\sigma = 5.67\times10^{-8}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4}

A body at temperature T in surroundings at T_s both emits and absorbs, so its net loss is

P_{net} = \varepsilon\sigma A(T^4 - T_s^4)

The fourth power makes the law dramatic: doubling the absolute temperature multiplies the radiated power by 2^4=16; trebling it multiplies it by 81.

Note that the curves are drawn normalised to their own peaks so that the shapes can be compared. In reality the total area under the 5000 K curve is (5/3)^4 = 7.7 times larger than under the 3000 K curve, and the peak intensity itself grows even faster, as T^5.

Wien's law

The wavelength at which the emission is strongest is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature:

\lambda_{max}T = b = 2.9\times10^{-3}\ \text{m K}

Body T (K) \lambda_{max} Region
Sun's surface 5800 500 nm visible (green-blue)
Tungsten filament 2800 1.0 μm near infrared
Human skin 310 9.4 μm infrared
Earth's surface 288 10 μm infrared

This is why the Sun looks white-yellow while a warm radiator glows dull red, and why infrared cameras can see people in the dark. It is also the basis of the greenhouse effect: the Sun's visible light passes through glass and the atmosphere, but the Earth's 10 μm infrared is absorbed by water vapour and carbon dioxide.

Worked example 8.3 — the Sun's peak wavelength

Problem. The Sun's surface is at about 5800 K. At what wavelength does it radiate most strongly?

Solution. \lambda_{max} = 2.9\times10^{-3}/5800 = 5.0\times10^{-7} m = 500 nm — green light, in the middle of the visible spectrum. Our eyes have evolved to be most sensitive near the peak of sunlight.

Worked example 8.4 — net radiation from a person

Problem. A person of surface area 1.5 m² and skin temperature 37 °C (310 K) stands in a room at 17 °C (290 K). Taking the emissivity of skin as 0.80, find the net rate of radiative heat loss.

Solution.

P = \varepsilon\sigma A(T^4-T_s^4) = (0.80)(5.67\times10^{-8})(1.5)(310^4-290^4)

310^4 = 9.24\times10^9 and 290^4 = 7.07\times10^9, so the bracket is 2.16\times10^9 K⁴.

P = 0.80\times5.67\times10^{-8}\times1.5\times2.16\times10^9 \approx 1.5\times10^2 W.

About 150 W — a useful check on why a room full of people warms up.

Putting the three modes to work

Device How it works
Thermos flask vacuum between the walls stops conduction and convection; the silvered walls have low emissivity, so radiation is reflected back
Double glazing the trapped air conducts poorly and the narrow gap suppresses convection
Solar cooker black absorbing surface, glass cover to trap radiation, insulation below
White clothes in summer low absorptivity, so most sunlight is reflected
Dark clothes in winter high absorptivity, so more solar energy is absorbed
Greenhouses glass transmits visible light but absorbs the outgoing infrared

Chapter summary

  • Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of molecules; thermal energy is the total internal energy (so it depends on mass); heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference.
  • Two bodies in thermal contact reach the same temperature — thermal equilibrium — with no net heat flow. The zeroth law makes "same temperature" transitive and so makes thermometry possible.
  • T=\theta_C+273 and \theta_F=\frac{9}{5}\theta_C+32; the scales agree at −40°; absolute zero is −273.15 °C.
  • Liquid-in-glass thermometers read the apparent expansion of the liquid; mercury covers −39 to 357 °C, alcohol −115 to 78 °C.
  • Resistance thermometers use R=R_0(1+\alpha\theta) and are the most accurate over a wide range; thermocouples use the Seebeck emf and are small, fast and wide-ranging; pyrometers measure radiation without contact.
  • Conduction obeys H=kA\Delta\theta/L; the temperature gradient is steepest in the poorer conductor, and thermal resistances L/kA add in series.
  • Convection is heat carried by a moving fluid; it needs gravity for the natural case.
  • Newton's law of cooling gives an exponential approach to the surroundings' temperature, with equal fractions of the excess lost in equal times.
  • A black body absorbs everything and is the best emitter; \varepsilon=\alpha. P=\varepsilon\sigma AT^4, and doubling T multiplies the power by 16.
  • Wien's law \lambda_{max}T=2.9\times10^{-3} m K puts the Sun's peak at 500 nm and a human's at about 9 μm.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (a) — heat is energy, so its unit is the joule. The watt is power and the kelvin is temperature.

2. (c) — 1 cal = 4.186 J; the calorie is the older unit of heat.

3. (d) — temperature measures the mean kinetic energy per molecule; the total internal energy also depends on the number of molecules.

4. (b) — the zeroth law makes thermal equilibrium transitive, so A and C must be at the same temperature.

5. (c) — absolute zero is 0 K, which is −273.15 °C.

6. (a) — 0 °C + 273 = 273 K.

7. (b) — 100 °C corresponds to 212 °F.

8. (d) — solving x=\frac{9}{5}x+32 gives x=-40.

9. (b) — a clinical thermometer covers only the narrow range of body temperature, 35–42 °C.

10. (a) — mercury solidifies at about −39 °C, which is why it cannot be used in very cold places; −115 °C is alcohol's freezing point.

11. (c) — the liquid expands more than the glass, so the thread rises; the reading is the apparent expansion.

12. (d) — R=R_0(1+\alpha\theta); the resistance is the thermometric property.

13. (a) — two junctions at different temperatures produce an emf by the Seebeck effect.

14. (c) — the total radiated power depends on T^4, so measuring it gives the temperature without contact.

15. (b) — from H=kA\Delta\theta/L, k has units W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.

16. (a) — silver has the highest thermal conductivity of the four, about 406 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.

17. (d) — a black body absorbs all radiation of every wavelength.

18. (c) — it is also the perfect emitter, by definition.

19. (a) — from P=\sigma AT^4, \sigma=P/(AT^4), W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

20. (b) — \lambda_{max}T=2.9\times10^{-3} m K.

21. (d) — radiation needs no medium; conduction and convection both need matter.

22. (c) — the rate is proportional to (\theta-\theta_s), not to the temperature itself.

23. (a) — the warmer liquid expands, becomes less dense and rises, and the cooler liquid sinks.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (d) — the same heat gives \Delta\theta=Q/mc, so the smaller mass has the larger rise; 1 kg rises twice as much.

2. (a) — it guarantees that a thermometer in equilibrium with a body reads that body's temperature.

3. (c) — equilibrium means equal temperatures, so the exchange rates are equal and there is no net flow; thermal energies can differ.

4. (c) — thermal energy depends on mass as well as temperature, and the bathtub has far more water.

5. (b) — mercury does not wet glass, so its thread stays clean and reads clearly. Alcohol wets glass and needs a dye.

6. (a) — alcohol freezes at about −115 °C, well below mercury's −39 °C.

7. (c) — platinum's resistance is stable and reproducible, so it can be calibrated to high accuracy over a wide range.

8. (a) — the junction is tiny, so it has a small heat capacity and responds quickly.

9. (a) — it needs no contact, so it can measure a moving belt or molten metal.

10. (a) — free electrons carry energy through the metal far faster than molecular vibration alone.

11. (b) — air has a very low conductivity, and a narrow gap prevents convection currents.

12. (c) — the heat current is the same through both, so \Delta\theta=HL/(kA) is largest where k is smallest.

13. (d) — P\propto T^4, and (600/300)^4=16.

14. (c) — Kirchhoff's law: at the same temperature and wavelength, absorptivity equals emissivity.

15. (d) — a white surface has low absorptivity, so it reflects most sunlight and stays cooler.
